frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over Sonatrach and pipeline exports, but European buyers are pressing for flexibility and lower long-term dependence. Hydrocarbon concentration still limits broader economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria’s non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Angola is reducing its exposure to Chinese lending, but oil-backed obligations and major infrastructure ties continue to constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and European support for the Lobito Corridor increases Angola’s strategic leverage while intensifying competition over access to Central African copper and cobalt supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER PIPELINE STANDOFF
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over border access and the operation of the Niger-Benin oil export route, putting transit revenues and regional energy cooperation at risk.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY FRONT
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from the Sahel is pressuring northern Benin and driving greater reliance on foreign security assistance and regional intelligence networks.

frictionVectors.title: DEBSWANA DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence through its partnership with De Beers, but diamond-market weakness and dependence on external marketing channels remain vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL DIVERSIFICATION RACE
frictionVectors.details: New coal, copper, and battery-mineral projects could broaden sovereign revenues, but foreign capital and infrastructure requirements will shape ownership outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING AND CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking tighter control over gold production and exports, but insecurity, informal mining, and illicit networks continue to divert value from public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The junta’s security partnership with Russia reduces reliance on Western actors but introduces new political and operational dependencies without resolving territorial insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Governance
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking greater state control and formalization of gold and nickel exports, but weak institutions and opaque trading networks limit revenue capture. Foreign buyers and regional intermediaries retain substantial leverage over supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda and eastern DRC constrain Burundi's strategic autonomy and raise the cost of securing transport corridors. External aid and regional security partnerships remain important buffers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is using its ports, air links, and maritime position to attract European and international investment, but this creates exposure to external operators and shifting Atlantic security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: External Economic Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, remittances, and concessional finance provide stability but leave the archipelago vulnerable to European demand, climate shocks, and foreign ownership of key infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Cameroon retains formal ownership of oil, gas, timber, and mining assets, yet foreign firms and trading networks capture significant value through production, logistics, and export access. Governance weaknesses and opaque contracting limit domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Affected Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies in the Far North and Anglophone regions threaten roads, pipelines, and agricultural corridors. The government remains dependent on external security, development, and infrastructure partners.

frictionVectors.title: Security-Mining Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The state relies heavily on Russian-linked security personnel and political support, while gold and diamond access remains a central component of the relationship. This strengthens regime survival but weakens transparent sovereign control over resources.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Poor transport links and insecurity along borders with Sudan, Chad, and Cameroon make exports dependent on external corridors and armed protection. Illicit taxation and smuggling continue to erode public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production and export infrastructure connected to neighboring Cameroon. International operators, lenders, and transit arrangements retain significant influence over revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are recalibrating ties with France and other Western partners while managing threats from Sudan, Libya, and armed groups in the Sahel. This increases bargaining room but also exposes the country to competing foreign security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies on foreign partnerships and diaspora ties for security, budget support, and maritime capacity. Competition among Gulf, French, and other external actors remains limited but politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource constraints
frictionVectors.details: Weak surveillance and limited port capacity constrain sovereign control over fisheries, shipping, and offshore resources. Dependence on external investment increases bargaining asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains heavily shaped by foreign firms, processing bottlenecks, and opaque subcontracting. Kinshasa is seeking greater local value addition but lacks sufficient infrastructure and enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Regional proxy conflict
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to undermine territorial control and mineral governance, with neighboring-state involvement and competing external diplomatic pressures. Transport corridors and mining zones remain vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export capacity remain strongly tied to hydrocarbons, leaving national bargaining power exposed to price cycles and foreign operators. Diversification into agriculture and processing remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and other external financing support roads, ports, and urban projects but can constrain fiscal autonomy. Debt-service pressures reduce the government's room to negotiate from strength.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: Growth in cocoa processing, mining, energy, and logistics is strengthening state capacity but remains reliant on multinational capital and imported technology. Abidjan is pursuing more domestic value addition without provoking investment flight.

frictionVectors.title: Northern border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel continues to pressure border infrastructure and security spending. Expanded regional coordination is improving resilience, though rural development gaps remain exploitable.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti converts its position near the Bab el-Mandeb into rent and diplomatic leverage through multiple foreign military facilities. The model boosts state revenue but leaves sovereignty exposed to great-power rivalry and regional conflict.

frictionVectors.title: External control of logistics assets
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and corridor infrastructure depends heavily on foreign finance, operators, and neighboring Ethiopia's trade demand. Debt exposure and competition among external partners constrain independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on Gulf investment, multilateral lending, and asset sales constrains Cairo's policy autonomy over strategic infrastructure and land. The state retains control of core assets but faces stronger external bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement. The dispute remains a major security concern despite ongoing diplomatic channels.

frictionVectors.title: Mature oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output increases dependence on foreign technical operators and new investment terms. State revenue remains vulnerable to production declines and volatile prices.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea is pursuing gas-processing and export partnerships to preserve its energy role, giving external firms significant influence over infrastructure and commercialization.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is increasingly valuable amid regional naval competition and insecurity around shipping routes. Foreign military interest creates leverage but also raises sovereignty and escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects rely on external capital and technical capacity under stringent state oversight. Sanctions exposure, labor concerns, and opaque contracting limit broader resource gains.

frictionVectors.title: Power and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini remains closely tied to South African electricity, transport, customs, and financial systems. Disruptions or policy shifts in South Africa can quickly affect domestic supply security.

frictionVectors.title: External investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: Manufacturing, sugar, and textile activity depends heavily on regional trade preferences and foreign investors. This limits diversification and leaves resource and industrial policy exposed to outside market decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam enhances Ethiopia's control over electricity generation but remains a source of acute tension with Egypt and Sudan. Operating disputes could intensify as filling and power exports progress.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF-backed reforms, and reliance on external financing constrain Addis Ababa's freedom over strategic infrastructure and exchange-rate policy. Conflict-related reconstruction further increases demand for outside capital.

frictionVectors.title: State Control of Extractives
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil and manganese operations. Implementation remains constrained by weak institutions and dependence on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port infrastructure remain closely tied to multinational mining interests, limiting Gabon's bargaining power over logistics and value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, underreported and foreign-controlled fishing continues to erode coastal resource sovereignty. Monitoring capacity remains insufficient relative to the scale of maritime activity.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on external donors and regional partners for roads, energy and security support, limiting fiscal and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illicit mining and smuggling weaken state revenue and environmental governance while foreign-linked supply chains retain substantial influence over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked fiscal reforms narrow policy space for local-content and industrialization measures. Emerging lithium and other critical-mineral projects will test Ghana's ability to secure domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale bauxite and iron-ore projects depend on foreign capital, consortiums and export infrastructure. Guinea's leverage is growing, but domestic processing and fiscal capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-Centered Contract Governance
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are renegotiating mining terms and demanding infrastructure commitments, but opaque decision-making and political uncertainty raise risks for sovereign accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cashew Trade
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains dependent on raw cashew exports, with foreign traders and processors capturing much of the value. Limited storage, finance and processing capacity weakens national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Fishing and Port Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement leaves fisheries vulnerable to foreign fleets and undermines revenue collection. Bissau's port and security environment also remain exposed to external political and criminal influence.

highlights: Port and Mineral Sovereignty Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy repayment obligations and reliance on multilateral financing constrain Nairobi's policy space. Infrastructure and budget choices remain sensitive to lenders including China and the IMF.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and energy projects offer strategic gains but raise concerns over land, security, and long-term control of transport corridors and mineral assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen bilateral dependence. Delays, cost overruns, and security around dams and tunnels expose Lesotho to external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Economic Enclavement
frictionVectors.details: South Africa dominates trade, energy access, transport routes, and employment flows. Limited diversification leaves Lesotho vulnerable to regional policy shifts and foreign-investor conditions.

highlights: Ports and Rail Corridors in Play

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign operators remain central to iron ore, gold, and related infrastructure, while Liberia seeks better fiscal returns and local value addition. Contract terms and environmental impacts remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and logistics networks shape access to Liberia's mineral hinterland. Weak domestic infrastructure limits Monrovia's bargaining power over concessionaires and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Divided Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks can disrupt fields, terminals, and export flows, weakening national control over the primary revenue source. International oil firms retain major operational influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and other external actors maintain security and commercial stakes through rival Libyan partners. Their presence complicates unified command over ports, airfields, and strategic energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Madagascar remains exposed to commodity cycles while capturing limited downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Energy, and Infrastructure Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Large mines and energy projects compete with local land rights and strained public utilities. Disputes over royalties, resettlement, and environmental impacts can undermine state legitimacy and project security.

highlights: Energy and fertilizer dependence remain binding

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but limited regulatory capacity risks leaving value capture and processing abroad. Government efforts to renegotiate terms face pressure from investors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy and Trade Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange scarcity, and dependence on regional transport routes constrain economic autonomy. Reliance on Mozambique and Tanzania-linked corridors leaves Malawi exposed to logistical and regional shocks.

highlights: Gold nationalism confronts external security dependence

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Mining Control
frictionVectors.details: The military government is asserting greater state control over gold operations and renegotiating foreign mining arrangements, creating friction with international operators. Production remains vulnerable to insecurity, opaque contracting, and smuggling.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security personnel and political backing reduces Western leverage but creates a new form of external dependency. Attacks by jihadist groups and deteriorating ties with regional organizations continue to threaten infrastructure and state reach.

highlights: Iron ore and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Development
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal is strengthening Mauritania's fiscal and strategic position, while also creating dependence on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and cross-border governance. Revenue management will determine whether gas improves sovereign control or reproduces enclave extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Atlantic Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and prospective green-hydrogen projects require large foreign-financed transport and energy infrastructure. Mauritania is balancing Gulf, European, Chinese, and other investors while trying to secure local value addition and control over ports and land.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains intertwined with the future of the strategically important Diego Garcia base. Any settlement must balance decolonization demands, U.S.-UK security interests, and Mauritian control of maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Blue Economy and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius depends on foreign capital, tourism, and imported energy while seeking greater control over fisheries, seabed resources, and port logistics. Competition among India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners provides leverage but also raises strategic balancing costs.

highlights: Renewables and phosphates strengthen strategic leverage
Western Sahara remains the central sovereignty contest

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure investment in Western Sahara while seeking wider international recognition of its autonomy framework. The Polisario Front, Algeria, and legal challenges to resource agreements remain persistent sources of friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale ports, railways, renewable projects, and industrial zones are supported by European, Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign capital. This expands Moroccan connectivity and bargaining power but leaves sensitive sectors exposed to competing external agendas.

highlights: LNG Restart Hangs on Cabo Delgado Security

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten LNG infrastructure and delay full-scale gas development. Mozambique relies heavily on foreign security assistance, limiting autonomous control of its resource frontier.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Local Content
frictionVectors.details: International operators retain major financial and technical leverage over gas projects. Expectations for domestic jobs, infrastructure, and revenue sharing remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Green Hydrogen Ambitions Gain Strategic Weight

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Oil and Hydrogen
frictionVectors.details: Namibia is attracting major international investors for offshore hydrocarbons and green hydrogen. The central challenge is converting capital inflows into durable state revenue, local ownership, and industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Water, Power, and Port Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on scarce water, expanded renewable generation, and upgraded ports. Infrastructure bottlenecks could increase reliance on foreign developers and neighboring supply networks.

highlights: Junta Reasserts Control over Uranium and Oil

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Contract Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control and value capture from uranium mining while relations with established foreign operators remain strained. Production uncertainty threatens export revenue and technical continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The transition away from French and Western security cooperation has increased reliance on Russian-linked personnel and equipment. This may strengthen regime autonomy in the short term while narrowing diplomatic and financial options.

highlights: Oil Theft Still Undermines State Control

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Vandalism and Oil Theft
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and insecurity continue to reduce production and public revenue. Foreign operators, state agencies, and local networks remain locked in a contested control environment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Finance and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs external capital and technology for gas, power, ports, and refining expansion. Financing terms and project ownership will determine whether infrastructure improves sovereignty or deepens dependence.

highlights: Mineral Transit Power Fuels Regional Leverage
Great Lakes Tensions Threaten Economic Diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: International scrutiny remains focused on alleged links between regional armed networks, mineral exports, and Rwanda's commercial channels. Diplomatic pressure risks sanctions, disrupted trade, and reduced investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development and security model remains supported by external finance and partnerships. Donor leverage is increasing as concerns grow over regional military activity and political restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea exploration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy firms remain central to offshore exploration, while uncertain commercial discoveries limit São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. Licensing must balance revenue hopes with environmental and sovereign-control concerns.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country's ports, energy system, and public investment pipeline depend heavily on external financing and technical partners, leaving limited room for autonomous infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil and gas projects
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, but international operators, financing structures, and midstream infrastructure still shape the pace and distribution of gains.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and opaque licensing remain a major sovereignty concern, threatening small-scale livelihoods and weakening domestic control over marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic competition in the Indian Ocean
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from partnerships with India, China, Gulf states, and Western actors, but port access, surveillance, and security cooperation can create pressure to align with competing external blocs.

frictionVectors.title: Marine-resource enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: The country's vast exclusive economic zone is difficult to patrol, allowing illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing to erode the value of its blue-economy strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain dependent on foreign capital, operators, and export logistics. Contract terms and revenue-sharing arrangements continue to determine whether resource wealth translates into durable national capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports rely on infrastructure controlled or financed by external partners, giving investors and lenders substantial influence over transport priorities and national development choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security architecture
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and Western partners provide security and port-related support, but their competing interests can constrain Mogadishu's independent control over strategic infrastructure and maritime policy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Potential hydrocarbons and valuable fisheries are complicated by weak enforcement, federal-regional disputes, and contested maritime authority. External firms and security actors are positioned to capture influence before Somali institutions consolidate control.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PROCESSING AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking more domestic beneficiation and strategic control over platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Foreign investment remains essential, creating tension between sovereignty goals and financing needs.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND POWER BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion, and freight-rail failures continue to weaken national control over mineral exports and raise dependence on private and external infrastructure providers.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese infrastructure to export nearly all of its oil, leaving revenue and sovereignty exposed to conflict, transit disruption, and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF RESOURCE REVENUES
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and unresolved power-sharing arrangements limit transparent management of oil income. Armed networks and neighboring states retain substantial leverage over production, transport, and security.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND ARMED ACTORS
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trading networks help finance rival wartime constituencies, while foreign commercial and security interests compete for access to Sudanese assets.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Conflict around transport corridors, refineries, and Port Sudan has made export infrastructure a strategic target. External mediation and logistical dependence increasingly shape access to national resources.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CONCESSION SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is expanding port and transport capacity while negotiating foreign participation in strategic corridors. The government must balance infrastructure finance with concerns over long-term control of trade gateways.

frictionVectors.title: MINING LOCAL-CONTENT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel, and other mineral projects are subject to stronger local-processing and revenue-sharing expectations. Disputes over licensing, taxation, and environmental safeguards remain a persistent friction point with foreign investors.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé provides strategic regional connectivity but depends heavily on foreign capital, operators, and shipping networks. This gives external partners influence over a critical national gateway.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal ownership of phosphate resources, yet limited domestic processing and financing constrain its ability to capture full value. Export dependence leaves the sector exposed to external market and buyer power.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European financial and migration partnerships while negotiations over external lending constrain policy autonomy. Fiscal stress limits the state's ability to manage strategic sectors independently.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons exposes Tunisia to price shocks and foreign supply conditions. Declining phosphate performance further weakens a historically important source of sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline is advancing under strong Chinese-linked construction and financing involvement, while Western environmental and human-rights opposition complicates access to capital and insurance.

frictionVectors.title: Export Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's future oil revenues depend on transit through Tanzania and broader regional stability. This gives external partners and neighboring states leverage over the country's resource-export strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Ownership and Tax Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater domestic value capture and stronger fiscal returns from copper and cobalt, but international mining firms retain major operational and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved fiscal room but leaves Zambia reliant on external creditors and partners for transport, power, and mining infrastructure. Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors is reshaping strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on unprocessed lithium exports, yet Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium, platinum, and other mining operations. Limited domestic capital and technology restrict the country's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted market access, and chronic currency instability raise dependence on non-Western financiers and informal trade channels. This weakens state bargaining power even as Harare pursues a resource-nationalist policy.
